name: Kirtipur
tagline: Hilltop Newar town 5 km from Kathmandu, with views and no crowds
meta_description: Kirtipur guide: hilltop Newar old town 5 km from Kathmandu, Bagh Bhairab and Uma Maheshwar temples, Chilancho stupa, Newari food and Chobhar gorge.
summary: Kirtipur is a Newar town on a ridge about 5 km south-west of central Kathmandu, at roughly 1,400 m. It has brick lanes, the Bagh Bhairab and Uma Maheshwar temples, the 16th-century Chilancho stupa and wide valley views. A half day covers the old town, a Newari lunch and nearby Chobhar gorge.
intro: Kirtipur is the old town we send people to when they ask where Kathmandu's Newar life still goes on without ticket booths and tour groups. It sits on a saddle between two low hilltops above Tribhuvan University, close enough to the city that you can see Swayambhunath and the Kathmandu skyline from its lanes, yet it feels a long way from Thamel. Farmers still dry grain in the squares in autumn, old men play cards outside rest houses, and the temples are used daily by the people who live around them.

The town's place in Nepali history is set by the siege of 1767. Prithvi Narayan Shah of Gorkha failed twice to take Kirtipur before it finally fell, and the victory opened the way to the conquest of the whole valley the following year. Accounts of the time describe harsh reprisals against the defenders. Swords and shields said to date from the fighting still hang on the walls of the Bagh Bhairab temple, and local guides tell the story with feeling, standing in the same lanes where it happened.

Practical Kirtipur is easy. The town is 30 to 45 minutes by car from Thamel, the old core can be walked in two hours, and the best Newari lunch in the area is served by a community-run kitchen near the main square. We usually pair Kirtipur with Chobhar gorge, 3 km away, or with the Chandragiri cable car base at Thankot, 12 km to the west. October to March brings dry lanes and clear views north toward Ganesh Himal and Langtang on good mornings.
facts: 1767 siege, Bagh Bhairab temple, Chilancho stupa, Newari food

highlights.title: Bagh Bhairab temple and its old weapons
highlights.text: Kirtipur's guardian is Bagh Bhairab, Shiva in tiger form, worshipped in a three-roofed temple at the centre of town. Swords and shields said to come from the 1767 siege hang on its outer walls, and animal sacrifices still take place on Saturdays and festival days. Visit quietly and ask before photographing worshippers.

highlights.title: Uma Maheshwar at the top of town
highlights.text: Climb the stone stairway to the northern hilltop and you reach the Uma Maheshwar temple, dedicated to Shiva and Parvati and flanked by a pair of stone elephants. The platform in front is the best viewpoint in Kirtipur, looking across Kathmandu to Swayambhunath and, on clear winter mornings, the white line of Ganesh Himal.

highlights.title: Chilancho stupa on the southern hill
highlights.text: The southern hilltop is crowned by the Chilancho stupa, a 16th-century Buddhist monument ringed by four smaller stupas and a cluster of courtyard monasteries. It is the Buddhist counterweight to the Hindu temples at the other end of town, and Newar Buddhists still circle it at dusk with prayer beads.

highlights.title: Brick lanes still used for daily life
highlights.text: Between the two hilltops runs a web of brick lanes, sunken water spouts and ponds, small squares and rest houses called pati. In October and November you will see grain spread out to dry on mats; in winter, women knit on doorsteps in the sun. It is the rhythm of an ordinary Newar town, with very few souvenir stalls.

highlights.title: Community-run Newari lunch
highlights.text: Kirtipur's best-known lunch stop is Newa Lahana, a community kitchen run by local women in traditional dress near the old town. It serves full Newari khaja sets with beaten rice, buffalo choila, bara lentil patties and pickles, and has become a favourite with Kathmandu families at weekends. Prices are modest and the food is cooked to order.

highlights.title: Chobhar gorge and Taudaha nearby
highlights.text: Three kilometres south-east, the Bagmati river cuts through the Chobhar gorge, the cleft that legend says Manjushri sliced to drain the valley lake. A 1903 iron footbridge, Ganesh and Lokeshwar temples and limestone caves sit around it. Taudaha pond, 2 km further south, draws migratory ducks from November to February.

how_to_reach.text: From Thamel, Kirtipur is ≈ 8–10 km and 30–45 minutes by car via the Ring Road at Balkhu, longer in evening traffic. The road climbs past Tribhuvan University to Naya Bazaar, where cars drop you at the edge of the old town. Local buses and microvans run from Ratna Park in central Kathmandu for about NPR 30–40, and a taxi costs roughly NPR 700–1,000 one way.

The old town is compact and best seen on foot: about 2 km of lanes and stone steps between the Uma Maheshwar and Chilancho hilltops. A gentle walk from Kirtipur down to Chobhar gorge takes 45 minutes to an hour along village roads, and the car can meet you at the bridge.

Tribhuvan International Airport is ≈ 14 km away on the far side of the city, roughly 45 minutes to an hour by car depending on traffic along the Ring Road. Kirtipur makes a sensible outing on a departure day for afternoon flights, as it avoids the congested old city centre.

where_to_stay: We rarely suggest sleeping in Kirtipur, because the town is so close to Kathmandu that a half-day trip covers it comfortably. Most of our guests stay in Thamel or Lazimpat for a central base, or in Patan's Jhamsikhel and Kupondole area, which is only about 6 km and 25 minutes from Kirtipur across the Bagmati. A few small hotels and guesthouses operate around Naya Bazaar and the university gate, used mainly by students and visiting academics; they are simple and suit budget travellers who want a quiet neighbourhood. Families wanting a hotel with a pool are better off in Kathmandu and driving out for the morning.
tips: Start from the top of town at Uma Maheshwar and walk downhill through the lanes to Bagh Bhairab and Chilancho, which saves your legs on the stairways.
Saturday mornings are busiest at Bagh Bhairab because of sacrifices; come on a weekday if blood rituals would upset you or your children.
Newa Lahana fills with Kathmandu families at weekend lunchtime, so aim for a weekday or arrive before 12 noon.
There was no town-wide visitor ticket at our last visit, but small donations at temples are welcome; check current status before you travel.
Pair Kirtipur with Chobhar gorge in the same half day, as the two are only 3 km apart and share the same approach road from Kathmandu.

experiences.title: Kirtipur old town walk with a local guide
experiences.price_hint: ≈ ₹2,000 per person with car from Kathmandu
experiences.summary: A two-hour walk across Kirtipur's two hilltops, from the Uma Maheshwar temple viewpoint through Newar lanes to Bagh Bhairab and the Chilancho stupa, with the story of the 1767 siege told along the way. Easy walking on brick lanes and stone steps.
body: We begin at the top. The car drops you near the northern ridge and a short stairway leads up to the Uma Maheshwar temple, guarded by stone elephants, with Kathmandu spread below. On a clear morning between October and February your guide can trace the line of the Himalaya from Ganesh Himal to Langtang behind the city haze. From here the walk is mostly downhill, which is why we start at this end rather than at Naya Bazaar.

The lanes below lead past sunken stone water spouts, Ganesh shrines on street corners and squares where grain is dried in autumn. At the Bagh Bhairab temple, your guide explains the tiger form of Shiva, the old weapons on the walls and the siege that ended Kirtipur's independence in 1767. It is a sober story, and locals still tell it with pride in the defenders. Allow time to sit in a pati rest house and watch the square; the best of Kirtipur is unhurried.

The walk ends at the southern hill, where the 16th-century Chilancho stupa rises from a ring of smaller stupas and Buddhist courtyards. The whole route covers about 2 km with a total height change of roughly 60 m, mostly on steps and brick lanes. It suits most ages, though the stairways have no handrails in places. Wear shoes that slip off easily for temple visits, and carry small notes for donations; check current status before you travel in case a visitor fee has been introduced.

faqs.q: Is Kirtipur worth visiting from Kathmandu?
faqs.a: Yes, especially if you want a Newar town without the crowds of the main Durbar Squares. Kirtipur is only 30 to 45 minutes from Thamel, the old town is walkable in two hours, and the temples, lanes and views give a real sense of daily life. It pairs well with Chobhar gorge or a Newari lunch.

faqs.q: What happened at the Battle of Kirtipur?
faqs.a: In 1767, after two failed attempts, Prithvi Narayan Shah's Gorkhali army captured Kirtipur following a long siege. Contemporary accounts describe severe punishment of the town's defenders. The fall of Kirtipur opened the way for the conquest of Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur in 1768 and 1769, forming the basis of the modern Nepali state.

faqs.q: How much walking is the Kirtipur heritage walk?
faqs.a: About 2 km over two to two and a half hours, including stops at temples and viewpoints. Most of it is on brick lanes and stone stairways with around 60 m of total height change, and we start at the top so most of the route is downhill. It is fine for children and most seniors with steady footing.

experiences.title: Newari khaja lunch in Kirtipur
experiences.price_hint: ≈ NPR 500–900 per person for a khaja set
experiences.summary: A full Newari khaja meal at a community-run kitchen in Kirtipur: beaten rice, buffalo choila, bara lentil patties, spiced potatoes, black soybeans and pickles, served on leaf plates by local women. A filling, inexpensive lunch and a good introduction to Newar food culture.
body: Newar cooking is the food of the Kathmandu Valley's original townspeople, and it is quite different from the dal bhat served in trekking lodges. Its centre is a khaja set, a snack meal built around beaten rice called chiura, with small portions of many dishes arranged around it. In Kirtipur we take guests to Newa Lahana, a kitchen run by women of the local community, who cook, serve and manage it together, often dressed in the black-and-red haku patasi sari.

A typical plate holds chiura, buffalo choila grilled and spiced with mustard oil, bara pancakes of ground black lentils, aloo tama with bamboo shoots, roasted black soybeans, boiled egg, and a sharp tomato or radish pickle. Vegetarians are well served: ask for a veg set with paneer or mushroom choila and extra bara. In winter, look for yomari, the steamed rice-flour dumplings filled with molasses and sesame that are eaten around Yomari Punhi in December. Locally brewed rice drinks are on the menu for those who want them.

A khaja set costs roughly NPR 500 to 900 per person, and portions are generous enough to replace lunch; check current status before you travel, as prices rise each year. The kitchen gets crowded at weekend lunchtimes with Kathmandu families, so we book weekdays or arrive by 12 noon. We usually schedule the meal at the end of the old town walk, when you have walked down the hill and earned it.

faqs.q: What is a Newari khaja set?
faqs.a: A khaja set is the classic Newar snack meal: a mound of beaten rice surrounded by small servings of spiced meat or vegetables, lentil patties, potato and bamboo-shoot curry, soybeans, egg and pickles. It is eaten with the hand or a spoon and is filling enough to replace lunch. Each dish is mildly to strongly spiced.

faqs.q: Is vegetarian Newari food available in Kirtipur?
faqs.a: Yes. Community kitchens in Kirtipur serve vegetarian khaja sets with beaten rice, bara lentil patties, potato curry, soybeans and pickles, often adding paneer or mushroom in place of buffalo choila. Tell us about Jain or no-onion-garlic needs in advance so we can ask the kitchen; those are possible but not standard.

faqs.q: Is the food at Newa Lahana safe for visitors?
faqs.a: In our experience, yes. The food is cooked fresh and served hot, which is the main safeguard. Stick to bottled or filtered water, go easy on raw salads and very spicy pickles on your first days in Nepal, and choose the cooked dishes. Guests with sensitive stomachs usually do well with the vegetarian set.

experiences.title: Chobhar gorge, iron bridge and hill temple
experiences.price_hint: Small fees for caves and park, ≈ NPR 100–300
experiences.summary: A short outing to Chobhar, 3 km from Kirtipur, where the Bagmati leaves the valley through a narrow gorge. Cross the 1903 iron footbridge, visit the Jal Binayak Ganesh temple and climb to Adinath Lokeshwar, hung with pots and pans offered by newly married couples.
body: Valley legend holds that the Kathmandu Valley was once a lake, and that the bodhisattva Manjushri cut a gap in the southern hills with his sword to let the water out. Chobhar gorge is that gap: a deep, narrow cleft through which the Bagmati river leaves the valley. Geologists agree on the lake, if not the sword, and the ancient lake sediments are why the valley floor is so fertile. Standing on the bridge, with the river squeezed between rock walls below, the story feels easy to believe.

The bridge itself is a piece of engineering history: a 1903 iron suspension footbridge with a span of about 40 m, made by Harpers of Aberdeen in Scotland and carried into Nepal in pieces. Beside the gorge stands Jal Binayak, a three-tiered Ganesh temple dating from the early 17th century. From the road, a short climb of about 15 minutes reaches the hilltop temple of Adinath Lokeshwar, sacred to Hindus and Buddhists, its walls covered with metal pots and pans offered by newlyweds hoping for a well-provisioned home.

Below the hill, the Chobhar caves can be explored with a local guide and a torch, and Manjushree Park has paths along the gorge; each charges a small entry fee, roughly NPR 100 to 300; check current status before you travel. Be prepared for one honest drawback: the Bagmati here carries Kathmandu's sewage, and the water smells in the dry season. Visit in the morning, then drive 2 km south to Taudaha pond, where ducks and other water birds winter from November to February.

faqs.q: What is the legend of Chobhar gorge?
faqs.a: Legend says the Kathmandu Valley was a great lake until the bodhisattva Manjushri cut through the southern hills with his sword at Chobhar, draining the water and making the valley habitable. Geologists confirm that a lake did once fill the valley. The gorge is where the Bagmati river still flows out today.

faqs.q: Can you walk on the Chobhar suspension bridge?
faqs.a: Yes. The 1903 iron footbridge, made by Harpers of Aberdeen in Scotland, is still used by pedestrians and spans about 40 m over the Bagmati. It sways slightly underfoot but is safe to cross at a normal pace. Hold small children's hands, and avoid crowding the deck when local groups are crossing.

faqs.q: Are the Chobhar caves suitable for children?
faqs.a: Older children who are comfortable in tight spaces usually enjoy them, but the caves involve crawling, wet rock and darkness, so they are not suitable for toddlers or anyone claustrophobic. Go with a local guide, carry a torch and wear clothes you do not mind getting muddy. Access can close after heavy rain.

faqs.q: How far is Kirtipur from Kathmandu?
faqs.a: Kirtipur is about 5 km south-west of central Kathmandu in a straight line and 8 to 10 km by road from Thamel. The drive takes 30 to 45 minutes via the Ring Road at Balkhu, depending on traffic. Local buses run from Ratna Park, and a taxi costs roughly NPR 700 to 1,000 one way.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee for Kirtipur?
faqs.a: At our last visit there was no town-wide visitor ticket for Kirtipur, unlike Bhaktapur or Patan Durbar Square. Temples accept donations, and the Chobhar caves and Manjushree Park nearby charge small fees. Municipal fees can be introduced or revised at short notice, so check current status before you travel.

Kirtipur is famous for its hilltop Newar old town, the 1767 siege by Prithvi Narayan Shah that preceded the conquest of the valley, the Bagh Bhairab temple, the Uma Maheshwar viewpoint and the Chilancho stupa. It is also home to Tribhuvan University, Nepal's oldest university, whose main campus spreads across the slopes below.

faqs.q: How much time do I need in Kirtipur?
faqs.a: A half day is right for most visitors: two hours for the old town walk, an hour for a Newari lunch, and an optional hour or two at Chobhar gorge. If you have only one full day for the western valley, we combine Kirtipur in the morning with the Chandragiri cable car in the afternoon.

faqs.q: Can I visit Kirtipur and Chandragiri in one day?
faqs.a: Yes. Kirtipur and the Chandragiri cable car base at Thankot are about 12 km apart, roughly 30 to 45 minutes by car. Spend the morning in Kirtipur with lunch, then ride up Chandragiri in the afternoon. Clouds tend to build by midday, so if mountain views matter most, reverse the order and go up Chandragiri first.

faqs.q: Is Kirtipur good for families with children?
faqs.a: Yes, with a little planning. The town is compact, traffic-free in the old lanes and full of things children notice: stone elephants, water spouts, pigeons and the swaying Chobhar bridge nearby. The stairways need care with toddlers, and Saturday sacrifices at Bagh Bhairab may upset younger children, so weekdays work better.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Kirtipur?
faqs.a: October to April is best, with dry lanes and the clearest views from October to February, when Kathmandu sits around 2 to 20 °C. Mornings give the best chance of seeing Ganesh Himal and Langtang from the Uma Maheshwar platform. The monsoon, June to September, brings afternoon rain and hazy views, though the town remains open.

Kirtipur is a residential town with a large student population and has a quiet, friendly feel, and we have no particular safety concerns there. Usual city sense applies: keep valuables zipped away and avoid dark lanes late at night. For the wider political situation in Kathmandu, check current advisories before you travel.

faqs.q: Where can I eat in Kirtipur?
faqs.a: The best-known option is Newa Lahana, a community-run Newari kitchen near the old town that serves khaja sets for roughly NPR 500 to 900. Small tea shops and momo stalls line the lanes around Naya Bazaar and the university gate. Restaurants serving Western food are scarce, so plan to eat Newari or Nepali food here.
